table_of_strategies.Definition: The time at which a patient with ischaemic symptoms is interpreted as presenting with ACS and ST-segment elevation (or ST-segment elevation equivalent).
Emergent PCI with balloon, stent, or other approved device, performed on the IRA without previous fibrinolytic treatment.
Emergency coronary angiography and PCI of the IRA if indicated.
Emergency PCI performed as soon as possible in cases of failed fibrinolytic treatment.

table_of_strategies.Strategy: Routine early PCI strategy after fibrinolysis
table_of_strategies.Definition: Coronary angiography, with PCI of the IRA if indicated, performed between 2 h and 24 h after successful fibrinolysis.
Fibrinolysis combined with rescue PCI (in cases of failed fibrinolysis) or routine early PCI strategy (in cases of successful fibrinolysis).
Emergency coronary angiography (i.e. as soon as possible) and PCI/CABG of the IRA if indicated.
Early coronary angiography (<24 h from diagnosis of ACS) and PCI/CABG of the IRA if indicated.
Coronary angiography ± PCI/CABG based on clinical assessment and/or non-invasive testing.

clinical_notes: CABG may also be indicated instead of PCI in certain circumstances.

AMI (acute myocardial infarction) is defined as cardiomyocyte necrosis in the clinical setting of acute myocardial ischaemia and includes MI due to atherothrombotic events (Type 1 MI) and other potential causes of myocardial ischaemia and myocyte necrosis (Type 2–5 MI).

Myocardial injury is a distinct entity used to describe troponin release due to mechanisms other than myocardial ischaemia and not meeting the criteria for MI; myocardial injury may be acute or chronic depending on evidence of change over time.
